subject: ela
cluster: Research to build and present knowledge
skillName: Draw evidence from literary or informational texts
description: Students draw evidence from literary and informational texts to support analysis, reflection, and research. Given a passage embedded inside the item, they locate the words, details, or examples in the text that best back up a stated claim, answer, inference, or analytical point. They distinguish strong, relevant, on-point textual evidence from quotations that are off topic, only loosely related, or that contradict the claim. They match a piece of evidence to the idea it supports, choose the best quotation to support a writing prompt or research question, and explain how a chosen detail proves the point. They apply this to literary texts (a story, poem, or play excerpt where evidence supports analysis of character, theme, or meaning) and to informational texts (an article or passage where evidence supports a factual claim, a main idea, or a research question). Because this is a writing and research standard built on reading, every item embeds the full passage or excerpt it depends on inside the item itself, so the student needs nothing external. Items test the components of finding and using evidence through analysis and selection rather than full multi-paragraph essays.
subSkills: Locate the specific words, lines, or details in a passage that directly support a given claim, answer, or inference
Distinguish strong, relevant evidence from quotations that are off topic, only loosely related, too general, or that contradict the claim
Match a piece of textual evidence to the idea, claim, character trait, or theme it supports
Choose the best quotation or detail from a passage to support a writing prompt or research question
Explain how a chosen piece of evidence proves or develops the point it is meant to support
Draw evidence from a literary text to support analysis of character, theme, plot, or the meaning of the text
Draw evidence from an informational text to support a factual claim, a main idea, or an answer to a research question
Recognize when a claim is unsupported by the text and identify what evidence would be needed to support it

problemArchetypes.name: Find the evidence for a claim (informational)
problemArchetypes.example: Read the short informational passage embedded in the item about how honeybees communicate by dancing. The item states a claim: 'Bees can tell each other where food is.' Which sentence from the passage best supports this claim? Answer: the sentence describing how a returning bee performs a waggle dance that points other bees toward the flowers, not a sentence that merely says bees live in hives or that they make honey.

problemArchetypes.name: Find the evidence for an analysis (literary)
problemArchetypes.example: Read the story excerpt embedded in the item. The item states an analysis: 'Maya is determined.' Which detail from the excerpt best supports this analysis? Answer: the detail showing Maya keeps practicing after she falls three times, not a detail that only tells what she is wearing or where she lives.

problemArchetypes.name: Choose the strongest evidence among quotations
problemArchetypes.example: Read the passage in the item, then read the prompt: 'Support the idea that the town worked together to clean the river.' Which quotation is the strongest evidence? Options give one on-point quotation, one off-topic quotation, one too-general quotation, and one that describes a single person acting alone. Answer: the quotation showing many residents joining the cleanup, because it directly supports the idea of the town working together.

problemArchetypes.name: Match the evidence to the idea it supports
problemArchetypes.example: Read the passage embedded in the item. The item lists a quotation: 'The lights flickered and the old house groaned in the wind.' Which idea does this evidence best support? Options: the setting feels eerie; the narrator is wealthy; the story takes place in summer; the narrator dislikes reading. Answer: the setting feels eerie, because the flickering lights and groaning house create a tense, spooky mood.

problemArchetypes.name: Explain how the evidence proves the point
problemArchetypes.example: Read the passage in the item and a claim with one chosen quotation. Which explanation best shows how the quotation supports the claim? Answer: an explanation that connects the specific words of the quotation to the claim, not one that restates the claim, summarizes the whole passage, or adds an opinion not found in the text.

problemArchetypes.name: Spot the unsupported claim or the irrelevant evidence
problemArchetypes.example: Read the passage embedded in the item. Which claim is NOT supported by the passage, or which quotation does NOT belong as evidence for the stated claim? Answer: the claim that has no matching detail in the text, or the quotation that is true but irrelevant to the point being argued.

Easy.description: A short passage of roughly 30 to 70 words embedded in the item, literary or informational, with a clearly stated claim or question. The task is identify-level: locate the one sentence or detail in the passage that directly and explicitly supports the claim, where the support is stated almost word for word. Only one component is tested and the correct evidence is unmistakable.
constraints: Stimulus is a 30 to 70 word passage included in the prompt
Claim is explicit and supported by a single clearly stated detail in the text
Identify-level task: locate the one directly supporting sentence or detail
Distractors are clearly weaker (a true but off-topic line, a detail about an unrelated part of the passage, a line that states the opposite)

Medium.description: A passage of roughly 70 to 130 words embedded in the item, literary or informational, paired with an analytical claim, an inference, or a research question. The task is analyze-level: choose the quotation or detail that best supports the point, or match a quotation to the idea it supports, where more than one option is plausible and the student must judge relevance and directness. Support requires light inference rather than a word-for-word restatement.
constraints: Stimulus is a 70 to 130 word passage in the prompt
Claim involves an inference, a character trait, a theme, or a research question rather than a literal restatement
Analyze-level task: weigh several plausible quotations and pick the most relevant, direct evidence
Distractors are plausible partial fits (evidence that is related but too general, evidence that supports a different idea in the passage, evidence that only partly addresses the claim)

Hard.description: A richer passage of roughly 130 to 220 words embedded in the item, literary or informational, with a more abstract analysis, a multi-part claim, or competing details. The task is evaluate-level: decide which quotation most strongly supports a nuanced analytical point, judge which explanation best shows how the evidence proves the claim, choose the strongest of two on-topic quotations, or identify an unsupported claim and the evidence it would need. Requires inference about author's purpose, theme, or how separate details combine to support a single point.
constraints: Stimulus is a 130 to 220 word passage included in the prompt
Claim is abstract or multi-part (theme, central idea, an inference that several details together support)
Evaluate-level task: select the strongest evidence or the best explanation of how evidence supports the claim, distinguishing among two or more on-topic options
Requires inference to judge relevance, sufficiency, and how the chosen detail connects to the larger analytical point

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student picks a detail that is true and in the passage but does not actually support the stated claim
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses an accurate, on-topic-sounding line from the text that is irrelevant to the specific point, because it appears in the same passage rather than because it proves the claim

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student selects evidence that is too general or vague instead of the specific detail that directly supports the claim
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Picks a broad summary sentence or a vague statement as the evidence instead of the precise detail that actually proves the point

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student chooses a line that contradicts or undercuts the claim, mistaking any related text for support
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects a quotation that states the opposite of the claim or shows a counterexample, treating mere topical overlap as support

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student matches evidence to the wrong idea, connecting a quotation to a different point made elsewhere in the passage
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Pairs a detail with an idea it does not support (for example, using a quotation about setting to support a claim about a character's motive)

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses summarizing the passage with explaining how evidence supports a claim
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses an explanation that retells the whole passage or restates the claim instead of showing how the specific words of the quotation prove the point

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student adds personal opinion or outside information as evidence rather than drawing on the text
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects an answer that brings in the student's own opinion or a fact not present in the passage instead of evidence taken from the text

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student treats an unsupported claim as supported, assuming a reasonable-sounding statement must be backed by the text
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Identifies a claim as supported when the passage contains no detail that proves it, because the claim sounds plausible

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student picks the first or most noticeable quotation rather than the strongest, most relevant evidence
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses a vivid or early line in the passage that catches attention over the less prominent line that more directly supports the claim
